latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: HLA-B51 and interacting antigen-processing risk alleles create a permissive background for Behcet disease by shaping mucosal and neutrophil-rich inflammatory responses.
Oral, genital, skin, and intestinal mucosal barrier disruption with microbial antigen exposure can trigger relapsing innate and adaptive immune activation.
Expanded Th1 and Th17 responses with TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17, IL-23, and impaired regulatory control amplify tissue inflammation across Behcet phenotypes.
Primed neutrophils show exaggerated chemotaxis, oxidative burst, degranulation, and NET formation, producing pathergy, pustular lesions, ulcers, and endothelial injury.
Endothelial activation, neutrophil adhesion, immune-mediated vessel-wall inflammation, and perivascular inflammation affect veins and arteries of all sizes.
Neutrophilic vascular reaction and ulcerative inflammation drive recurrent oral aphthae, genital ulcers, erythema nodosum-like lesions, papulopustules, and pathergy.
Relapsing nongranulomatous anterior/posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis, occlusive vasculitis, and macular edema cause cumulative irreversible visual damage.
Venous wall inflammation and endothelial injury produce deep vein thrombosis, superficial thrombophlebitis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and Budd-Chiari syndrome.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Arterial vasculitis with aneurysm and pseudoaneurysm formation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Transmural arterial inflammation weakens vessel walls, causing pulmonary artery aneurysm, peripheral pseudoaneurysm, aortic involvement, thrombosis, rupture, and massive hemorrhage.
Parenchymal brainstem-diencephalic meningoencephalitis, myelitis, or non-parenchymal cerebral venous sinus thrombosis cause neurologic deficits, headache, and disability.
Deep oval ileocecal and colonic ulcers with neutrophilic vasculitic inflammation drive abdominal pain, diarrhea, bleeding, perforation, and stricturing.
Sterile neutrophil-predominant synovitis produces recurrent oligoarthritis or polyarthritis, usually non-erosive and self-limited.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: HLA-B51 and antigen-processing risk alleles bias immune activation toward Behcet-type inflammatory responses.
Mucosal antigen exposure and microbial dysbiosis stimulate Th1/Th17 cytokines and innate inflammation in genetically susceptible patients.
TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-8, IL-17, and GM-CSF prime neutrophils for chemotaxis, oxidative burst, adhesion, and NET formation.
Neutrophil-rich vascular reaction explains aphthae, pustules, erythema nodosum-like lesions, and pathergy.
Cytokine-driven endothelial activation recruits neutrophils and mononuclear cells to vessel walls.
NETs, degranulation, and endothelial adhesion amplify vascular injury and thrombosis.
Retinal and uveal vascular inflammation produces relapsing uveitis and occlusive retinal vasculitis.
Inflammation of venous walls is the main driver of thrombosis in Behcet disease.
Transmural arterial inflammation weakens arterial walls and promotes pseudoaneurysm or aneurysm formation.
Behcet-related CNS disease includes inflammatory brainstem parenchymal disease and venous sinus thrombosis.
Intestinal Behcet lesions share mucosal Th1/Th17 inflammation and neutrophilic ulceration.
Inflammatory cytokines and neutrophil-rich synovitis produce recurrent non-erosive arthritis.
Recurrent painful oral aphthae are the most common mucocutaneous expression.
Genital aphthae are Behcet-characteristic mucosal ulcers and often scar.
Panniculitis-like tender nodules are common, especially in women.
Sterile acneiform papulopustules reflect neutrophilic follicular inflammation.
Needle trauma triggers exaggerated neutrophilic papule/pustule formation in pathergy-positive patients.
Nongranulomatous anterior uveitis and hypopyon occur during ocular flares.
Posterior segment inflammation is a major driver of visual morbidity.
Retinal vasculitis, often occlusive, is characteristic and predicts visual loss.
Posterior uveitis and retinal vasculitis can cause cystoid macular edema.
Repeated posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis, and macular edema cause irreversible visual decline.
Lower-extremity DVT is a common vascular expression of Behcet disease.
Non-parenchymal neuro-Behcet can present with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and intracranial hypertension.
Inflammatory thrombosis can recur or extend without control of vascular inflammation.
Pulmonary artery aneurysm is a classic life-threatening arterial manifestation.
Pulmonary artery aneurysm can rupture and cause massive hemoptysis.
Parenchymal CNS disease and venous sinus thrombosis produce focal deficits, pyramidal signs, cranial neuropathies, and altered mental status.
Parenchymal neuro-Behcet has risk of residual neurologic disability and relapse.
Deep ileocecal ulcers are the central lesion of intestinal Behcet disease.
Deep intestinal ulcers can bleed or perforate.
Recurrent sterile inflammatory arthritis commonly affects knees, ankles, wrists, and elbows.
Systemic inflammatory activity raises CRP, especially with vascular, intestinal, or arthritis flares.
Deaths in Behcet disease are mainly mediated by pulmonary artery aneurysm hemorrhage, major vascular disease, neurologic disease, intestinal perforation, and treatment-related infection.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Oral and genital ulcers are often co-expressed in mucocutaneous flares, although either can occur alone.
Erythema nodosum-like lesions and arthritis commonly cluster in less organ-threatening inflammatory flares.
Anterior uveitis produces eye pain, redness, and photophobia.
Occlusive retinal vasculitis is the most important short-term predictor of irreversible visual damage.
Macular edema directly impairs central vision and may cause persistent visual decline.
Pulmonary artery aneurysm commonly presents with hemoptysis, but thrombosis and inflammation can also contribute.
Larger or expanding pulmonary artery aneurysms carry high rupture and massive hemoptysis risk.
Hemoptysis may be the warning sign immediately preceding life-threatening pulmonary arterial hemorrhage.
Deep intestinal ulcers cause abdominal pain, often in the ileocecal region.
Deep, large, or refractory intestinal ulcers can bleed or perforate.
Parenchymal neuro-Behcet lesions produce neurologic deficits.
Parenchymal neuro-Behcet can leave persistent deficits, especially with delayed or incomplete control.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis commonly causes headache and intracranial hypertension.
Both are nonspecific acute phase markers, with CRP changing more rapidly than ESR.
Massive hemoptysis, aneurysm rupture, and intestinal hemorrhage are major causes of death.
Intestinal perforation can cause peritonitis, sepsis, surgery, and death.
High-intensity immunosuppression and biologics raise serious infection risk, which can dominate mortality in older or comorbid patients.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Local anti-inflammatory therapy is most useful for active accessible ulcers.

failure_modes: secondary candidiasis with prolonged oral use

side_effects.interpretation: Symptomatic improvement rather than disease-modifying control

treatments.context_specific_role: Local control of oral and genital ulcers; does not protect eye, vascular, neuro, or intestinal organs.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Colchicine is particularly useful for erythema nodosum-like lesions and articular disease.
Dose reduction or avoidance is needed in severe renal impairment due to neuromyopathy and marrow toxicity.
Often considered usable in pregnancy when benefits outweigh risks, but dose and local practice vary.

failure_modes: myopathy or neuropathy especially with renal impairment or CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors
inadequate for eye, vascular, neurologic, or severe intestinal disease

side_effects.interpretation: Rare marrow suppression, higher risk with renal impairment or interacting drugs

treatments.context_specific_role: Systemic mucocutaneous and articular control, especially erythema nodosum-like lesions, genital ulcers, and arthritis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Evidence is strongest for reducing oral ulcer number and pain.
Dose adjustment is required in severe renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral ulcer-predominant Behcet disease when local therapy and colchicine are inadequate or unsuitable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Azathioprine reduces ocular relapse frequency and is used for ocular involvement.
Azathioprine is one of the immunosuppressives most often continued in pregnancy when needed.
Hepatotoxicity and marrow suppression require close monitoring or avoidance.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing immunosuppression for ocular, vascular, intestinal, and recurrent systemic disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Uncontrolled infection raises risk; organ-threatening Behcet may still require steroids with antimicrobial/source control.
Rapid suppression is needed for acute sight-threatening ocular inflammation.
High-dose steroids are used with cytotoxic or biologic therapy for life-threatening arterial inflammation.

failure_modes: relapse during taper if not combined with steroid-sparing therapy
treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid flare suppression for ocular, vascular, neurologic, intestinal, and severe mucocutaneous disease; rarely sufficient alone for organ-threatening disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Infliximab or adalimumab can rapidly suppress refractory or sight-threatening uveitis and retinal vasculitis.
Anti-TNF therapy is effective for refractory intestinal Behcet disease.
Latent TB screening and prophylaxis are required before TNF blockade.
HBV reactivation risk requires antiviral prophylaxis or hepatology-directed treatment planning before TNF blockade.
Chronic HCV requires liver-safety assessment and antiviral treatment planning before sustained immunosuppression.
Anti-TNF agents can worsen demyelinating disease.
Anti-TNF agents can worsen advanced heart failure.

failure_modes: loss of response due to anti-drug antibodies

side_effects.interpretation: Serious infection and TB reactivation risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Severe or refractory ocular, intestinal, vascular, neurologic, and mucocutaneous Behcet disease, especially when rapid steroid-sparing control is needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cyclosporine can suppress ocular Behcet inflammation.
Cyclosporine is associated with increased risk of neurologic involvement and is avoided when neuro-Behcet is present.
Nephrotoxicity and hypertension require avoidance or careful monitoring.

side_effects.interpretation: Neurotoxicity or association with neuro-Behcet risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Ocular Behcet option when neuro-Behcet is absent and renal/BP toxicity is acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Interferon-alpha has evidence for refractory ocular Behcet disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Refractory ocular and mucocutaneous disease when anti-TNF or conventional immunosuppression is unsuitable or ineffective.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Life-threatening pulmonary artery aneurysm requires aggressive suppression of arterial wall inflammation.
Cyclophosphamide is gonadotoxic and teratogenic; use only in life-threatening settings with specialist input.
Severe infection risk rises substantially with cytotoxic therapy and steroids.

treatments.context_specific_role: Aggressive induction for pulmonary artery aneurysm, severe arterial disease, or severe neuro-Behcet when risk justifies cytotoxic therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Used for mild to moderate intestinal Behcet inflammation, especially colonic/ileocecal symptoms.

side_effects.interpretation: Rare interstitial nephritis or renal toxicity

treatments.context_specific_role: Mild to moderate intestinal involvement; escalation needed for deep, refractory, bleeding, or perforation-risk ulcers.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pulmonary artery aneurysm must be excluded or controlled before anticoagulation because massive hemoptysis risk can dominate.
Active bleeding, large aneurysm, or severe intestinal bleeding precludes anticoagulation.
Anticoagulation is often considered in cerebral venous sinus thrombosis after bleeding risks are assessed.

failure_modes: recurrent thrombosis if inflammation remains active
treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for selected venous thrombosis after aneurysm/bleeding risk assessment; vascular inflammation still requires immunosuppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active arterial inflammation increases postoperative pseudoaneurysm and graft complication risk; immunosuppression around intervention is essential.
Life-threatening hemoptysis or rapidly enlarging aneurysm may require urgent endovascular/surgical control.

failure_modes: relapse at anastomosis if inflammation uncontrolled
treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical control of high-risk aneurysm or rupture risk, coordinated with aggressive immunosuppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IL-1 blockade can benefit refractory mucocutaneous and systemic inflammatory flares in selected patients.
Active serious infection should be controlled before IL-1 blockade.

treatments.context_specific_role: Selected refractory mucocutaneous or systemic inflammatory disease when conventional agents and anti-TNF are unsuitable or insufficient.

turkish_middle_eastern_mediterranean_cen.trajectory_modulation: Higher prevalence in populations along historical Silk Road regions; phenotype mix varies by region.

northern_european_ancestry.trajectory_modulation: Lower prevalence; diagnosis still possible with compatible clinical pattern.

axis_response_modulation.M_BEHCET_TH1_TH17_TNF_IL1_AXIS: higher flare amplitude and more classic mucocutaneous/ocular clustering in some cohorts

young_adult_onset_15_35.trajectory_modulation: Typical onset window; organ-threatening ocular/vascular disease often declares early.

childhood_onset.trajectory_modulation: Less common but may have familial/autoinflammatory overlap and severe course.

late_onset_over_50.trajectory_modulation: Lower prior; consider mimics while retaining compatible disease if recurrent aphthae plus systemic pattern is strong.

male.trajectory_modulation: Male sex, especially young onset, is associated with more severe ocular, vascular, neurologic, and mortality risk.

female.trajectory_modulation: Mucocutaneous and articular clusters may predominate in many cohorts; severe disease still occurs.

positive_first_degree_family_history.trajectory_modulation: Familial clustering is stronger in high-prevalence regions and pediatric-onset disease.

frequent_recurrent_oral_aphthae.trajectory_modulation: Strongly raises prior when combined with genital ulcers, ocular inflammation, skin lesions, vascular, neurologic, or intestinal disease.

current_smoker.trajectory_modulation: Associations vary; smoking worsens vascular and cardiopulmonary risk and complicates mucosal healing.

axis_response_modulation.M_BEHCET_MUCOSAL_MICROBIAL_TRIGGER: higher baseline and easier flare triggering

recent_infection_or_mucosal_trauma.trajectory_modulation: May trigger aphthous or systemic flare in susceptible patients.

prior_ocular_involvement.trajectory_modulation: Raises relapse and cumulative vision-loss risk; requires ophthalmology surveillance.

prior_vascular_involvement.trajectory_modulation: Raises recurrence and mortality risk; anticoagulation decisions must account for aneurysm risk.

prior_neuro_behcet.trajectory_modulation: Raises relapse and disability risk; cyclosporine is generally avoided.

pregnancy_or_postpartum.trajectory_modulation: Disease course is variable; treatment selection changes because cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, mycophenolate, thalidomide, and some biologic timing decisions are constrained.

recent_stop_of_immunosuppression.trajectory_modulation: Raises relapse risk for ocular, vascular, neurologic, and intestinal disease after previous control.

supportive_care: Regular rheumatology follow-up with phenotype-specific surveillance for mucocutaneous, ocular, vascular, neurologic, intestinal, and articular involvement.
Urgent ophthalmology evaluation for any eye pain, redness, photophobia, floaters, or visual change; slit lamp, OCT, and fluorescein angiography when posterior involvement is suspected.
CT or MR angiography when hemoptysis, chest pain, unexplained dyspnea, large-vessel thrombosis, or arterial aneurysm is suspected; exclude pulmonary artery aneurysm before anticoagulation.
Neurology evaluation and brain/spine MRI plus MRV/CTV for severe headache, papilledema, focal deficits, brainstem signs, myelopathy, or altered mental status.
Gastroenterology evaluation with ileocolonoscopy and imaging for persistent abdominal pain, diarrhea, GI bleeding, weight loss, anemia, or suspected perforation.
Oral hygiene optimization, dental care, avoidance of mucosal trauma where possible, topical analgesics, and nutrition support during severe oral ulcer flares.
Skin and genital ulcer wound care; screen for superinfection or sexually transmitted infections when clinically appropriate without using infection absence as a diagnostic shortcut.
Vaccination review before immunosuppression: inactivated influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, HBV, HPV, and recombinant zoster as appropriate; avoid live vaccines during significant immunosuppression.
TB, HBV, HCV, and HIV screening before anti-TNF, high-dose steroids, cyclophosphamide, or other high-risk immunosuppression; prophylaxis or treatment when indicated.
CBC, liver enzymes, creatinine, urinalysis, CRP, and ESR monitoring tailored to medication and organ phenotype.
Fertility preservation and contraception counseling before cyclophosphamide or teratogenic therapies; pregnancy planning with rheumatology and maternal-fetal medicine.
Bone protection, glucose monitoring, blood pressure control, and infection counseling during glucocorticoid treatment.
Multidisciplinary care for vascular Behcet involving rheumatology, vascular surgery/interventional radiology, pulmonology, and hematology when anticoagulation is considered.
Physical therapy, neurorehabilitation, and occupational therapy after neurologic flares or severe arthritis.
Patient education on red flags: sudden visual loss, severe eye pain, hemoptysis, neurologic deficit, severe headache, chest pain, melena/hematochezia, acute abdomen, and unilateral leg swelling.
